Repeat Criteria
Tags: courses
Short Description: The criteria specifying how many times a course may be taken, the maximum credits that may be earned through repeated enrollment, and any restrictions on repeating the course within the same term.
Repeat Criteria
The criteria specifying the limits and conditions for repeating a course, including:
Maximum Enrollments: The maximum number of times a course may be taken.
Maximum Credits Allowed: The maximum number of credits that may be earned through repeated enrollment during a student’s academic career.
Same-Term Repeats: Whether the course may be repeated within the same term.
Maximum Credits Allowed Per Term: The maximum number of credits that may be taken through repeat enrollment in a single term.

Level
Tags: programs,specializations
Short Description: The academic level of a curricular offering (undergraduate / graduate / dual)
Level
Level identifies the academic level of a curricular offering.

Undergraduate: Courses numbered 499 and below.
Graduate — Courses numbered 500 and above.

Undergraduate: A program leading to an undergraduate degree or credential, such as a bachelor’s degree, undergraduate certificate, or minor.
Graduate: A program designed for students who have completed a bachelor’s degree and are pursuing graduate or post-baccalaureate study, including master’s degrees, doctoral degrees, graduate certificates, and other post-baccalaureate credentials.

In addition to undergraduate and graduate, proposers may select Dual for programs that provide an accelerated pathway connecting a bachelor's and master's degree, including ABM and 4+1 specializations.
Related toolkit entry: ABM
Related toolkit entry: 4+1
ABM (Accelerated Bachelor to Master's): A pathway that allows students to double-count eligible courses toward both the bachelor's and master's degrees, reducing the time required to complete the master's degree
Kuali: ABM programs are inherited from the master's degree.
4+1: A pathway that allows students to complete both a bachelor's and master's degree in five years. Unlike an ABM, a 4+1 does not include double-counted courses.
Kuali: 4+1s are inherited from the bachelors degree.

New Program Proposal Walkthrough
New Program Proposal Walkthrough
This guide provides step-by-step procedural instructions for completing and submitting a New Program Proposal in Kuali. It focuses on navigating the form, including what to select or enter in each field.
*In Kuali, Programs refer to Degrees, Majors, Minors & Certificates.
The guide is organized by proposal section (panel), so you can jump directly to a section when you need help.
This guide does not provide guidance on course content or academic decisions. Consult your department and applicable curriculum committees for questions about developing the course itself.
Navigate by Section

Familiarize yourself with URI’s curricular process before beginning your proposal. This will help you understand the steps involved in the curricular process and accurately estimate how long your proposal may take to reach approval.
How the Curriculum Process Works

From your browser, navigate to Kuali Curriculum Management (CM).

Additional Proposer(s) Use this section to identify additional individuals who can speak to the proposed program. Individuals listed here will not receive Kuali notifications or have access to edit the proposal. Their inclusion simply provides transparency to the reviewing committees about who else is involved in or can speak to the proposal.

Effective Term & Year Select the term and year in which you intend the program to become effective. If the selected effective term has passed the applicable deadline by the time the proposal reaches the Faculty Senate, it will automatically be updated to the next available term.

Understand the Workflow
Understand the Workflow

The curriculum approval process generally follows the sequence shown in the URI Curricular Approval Process Flowchart. Specific steps may vary by college, department, proposal type, and whether the proposal requires additional levels of review.
URI Curricular Approval Process Flowchart

Proposal Development Faculty use the forms in Kuali Curriculum Management to develop the proposal and work with other stakeholders as appropriate.
Department Review The proposal is reviewed through the appropriate departmental process.
College Curriculum Committee Review The College Curriculum Committee reviews the proposal.
College Dean Approval The College Dean approves the proposal for Faculty Senate review.
Faculty Senate Curriculum Committee Review The Curriculum & Standards Committee, the General Education Committee, or the Graduate Council reviews the proposal.
Faculty Senate Approval The Faculty Senate considers the curriculum committee's recommendation and votes.
University President Approval Any curricular item that is not a course must be reviewed and approved by the University President.
URI Board of Trustees Approval In addition to the University President’s approval, new Majors and Degrees are also reviewed by the Board of Trustees.

While all Colleges follow the curriculum approval process established in the University Manual, each College may have its own internal approval process based on its departmental and governance structures. To download a flowchart of a specific College’s approval process, select the College below.

Instructional Delivery Method
Tags: courses
Short Description: The instructional delivery method. Also known as "method of instruction.”
Instructional Delivery Method
Provided below is the complete list of approved methods of instruction, as proposed in FSEC Report #2024-2025-03 and subsequently approved by the Faculty Senate through Bill #24-25-12 on January 23, 2025.
A course in which the primary method is presentation and students are expected to participate in a variety of ways, such as small-group discussions, questions and answers, writing-exercises, etc.
Applied course work, generally involving experimentation or observation, typically using special equipment (including computers and specialized software).
Separate sections of a lecture course regularly scheduled for discussion.
Supervised work with an emphasis on performance and creativity in which faculty instruct, assist, and critique.
Course offered to a small group (usually no more than 20 students) where participants actively exchange ideas and findings based on readings or research.

One-on-one instruction in which the student enters into an agreement with the instructor that defines the focus of inquiry and nature of activities. Includes tutorials, directed readings, special projects.
Structured experiences where the primary aim is to connect theory with practice. Includes clinics, internships, externships, student teaching, field experiences. May include regular class meetings.
Similar to a seminar, with emphasis on applied rather than theoretical learning, but not offered for degree-program credit.
